characters: JESUS (never show his face; always from behind, hands only, or a small distant figure): a man of about 33, shoulder-length dark-brown wavy hair, short dark beard seen only at the edge of the jaw from behind, undyed cream linen tunic with a faded blue-grey wool mantle over one shoulder, worn leather sandals, olive-brown working hands. PETER (days 2 and 5): a broad fisherman in his early 40s, weathered tanned face, short grey-streaked black curly hair, thick full black-and-grey beard, heavy brown wool tunic with a rope belt, big rough hands. THE OTHER DISCIPLES: men aged 18 to 50, earth-tone wool tunics (sand, olive, rust), mixed beards; one young beardless one. TERTULLIAN (day 1): a North African Roman man of about 50, dark olive skin, close-cropped black-and-grey hair, short trimmed beard, white wool pallium draped over a tunic, reed pen. THE PRODIGAL SON (day 3): about 19, thin, dark messy hair, first in a rich red tunic with a gold-trimmed belt, later in a torn, dirty ochre tunic, barefoot. HIS FATHER (day 3): about 65, long white beard, white hair, long indigo robe and sash. PAUL OF PHERME (day 4): an old Egyptian desert monk, gaunt, bald head, long white beard, patched brown wool habit, barefoot. MACARIUS (day 4): very old and small, bald, wispy white beard, deep-set kind eyes, dark brown hooded robe, leaning on a palm-wood staff. JUAN DIEGO (day 7): a Nahua man of about 57, brown skin, straight black hair to the collar streaked with grey, no beard, plain white cotton shirt and trousers, a rough pale-beige agave-fiber cloak (tilma) knotted at one shoulder, sandals. THE LADY OF GUADALUPE (day 7): as in the traditional image: a young woman with brown skin and dark hair, head bowed, hands joined, rose-colored dress with gold flowers, turquoise mantle scattered with gold stars, gold rays of light around her. BISHOP ZUMARRAGA (day 7): Spanish Franciscan of about 60, grey-brown habit with a white cord, grey beard, plain pectoral cross. TODAY FAMILY (the last picture of every film, same people every day): MATEO, 17, Mexican-American, short black fade haircut, light stubble, grey team hoodie or white-and-navy baseball uniform; his sister LUCIA, 15, long dark wavy hair, oversized denim jacket, small gold cross necklace; their ABUELA, about 72, silver hair in a low bun, glasses, maroon cardigan, a wooden rosary; their dad MIGUEL, late 40s, short greying hair, mustache, work jacket; and Mateo's friend GRACE, 16, Filipino-American, black bob haircut, round glasses, cream sweater.

1.story: The sending on the mountain, Matthew 28:16-20, and Christians tracing the cross on their foreheads, Tertullian, De Corona 3 (around 200)
1.point: The sign of the cross is an ancient two-second prayer: the hand traces the cross over all of you while the words name one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
1.script: A hill in Galilee. Eleven friends climb it to meet Jesus, risen from the dead. Some of them still doubted. He sends them anyway. Go to every nation, he says, and baptize, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Less than two hundred years later, a writer named Tertullian noticed something. Christians traced a tiny cross on their foreheads all day. Getting dressed. Sitting down to eat. Lighting a lamp. That tiny cross grew into this one. The hand traces the cross Jesus died on. The words name one God. Forehead, chest, shoulder, shoulder: where you think, feel and carry. That's why a pitcher does it before the first throw. All of you, in two seconds.

open.text: the smallest prayer is *1,800 years* old.

beats: Less than two hundred years later
pictures: Picture 1: A green hilltop in Galilee at early morning, the Sea of Galilee shining far below. Eleven men in earth-tone wool tunics climb the last stretch of a rocky path, some eager, some hanging back. At the summit, small and far away, Jesus stands with his back to us in a cream tunic and blue-grey mantle, soft gold light around him. Wide vertical framing, path leading up the frame.

Picture 2: Over Jesus's shoulder, from behind (only his hair, mantle and one raised hand visible), the eleven stand in a loose half-circle on the hilltop. Peter leans forward, eager; two men at the edge stand with arms folded, frowning, unsure. Wind in their cloaks. Morning light on their faces. Medium vertical framing.

Picture 3: Carthage, North Africa, around the year 200. A whitewashed Roman room at night lit by a small clay oil lamp. Tertullian, in a white pallium, sits at a wooden table writing on a scroll with a reed pen, looking up thoughtfully toward an open window where a city street glows. Warm amber light, deep shadows.

Picture 4: Inside a modest Roman North African home at dawn, a young mother of about 25 in a simple blue tunic and pale headscarf, half-dressed for the day, presses her thumb to her forehead to trace a tiny cross, eyes closed. Beside her a small child at a low table with bread copies her. A clay lamp is being lit on a shelf. Close, intimate vertical framing, soft gold light.

Picture 5: A close, simple painting of a pair of hands mid-gesture making the large sign of the cross: fingertips at the forehead, with soft ghosted traces showing the path down to the chest and across the shoulders, the gesture glowing faintly like light. Background: warm candlelit stone of an old church, holy water font in soft focus. No face needed, just the shoulders and hands of a young person in a hoodie.

Picture 6: TODAY. A high-school baseball game at golden hour. Mateo, 17, in a white-and-navy uniform, stands on the pitcher's mound, glove under his arm, touching his right shoulder as he finishes the sign of the cross, eyes down, calm. In the bleachers behind the fence, Lucia in her denim jacket and Abuela in her maroon cardigan watch, Abuela smiling. Warm, real, cinematic.
motion: Slow push up the path toward the distant figure on the summit while the men's cloaks and the grass ripple in the wind.
Gentle sideways drift across the half-circle of faces as Jesus's raised hand holds still and the wind moves their hair.
Lamp flame flickers and shadows breathe on the wall while the camera eases slowly toward Tertullian as he lifts his pen.
The mother's thumb slowly traces the small cross on her forehead as the child copies her and the lamp catches light; slight push in.
The hand moves smoothly from forehead to chest to left shoulder to right, leaving a soft fading trail of light; camera holds still.
Mateo completes the sign and looks up toward home plate as a breeze moves the bleacher banners; slow push in from the infield.

2.story: The living bread and the followers who walked away, John 6:22-69; the Last Supper, Luke 22:19
2.point: Catholics believe the Eucharist is not a symbol but Christ himself, truly present, which is why he is believed to stay in the tabernacle beside the red lamp.
2.script: A crowd chased Jesus across the lake. He'd just fed thousands with five loaves. Now he told them: I am the living bread. Whoever eats this bread will live forever. And the bread I give is my flesh. People argued. His own followers said: this is too hard. And many of them walked away. He didn't call them back. He let them go. Then he turned to his twelve: will you leave too? Peter said: Lord, to whom would we go? At his last supper, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, and said: this is my body. Gave thanks, in Greek: eucharistia. Catholics believe that at every Mass, the bread truly becomes him. Not a symbol. Him. The red lamp in an empty church? He stayed.

open.text: his followers *walked away.* he let them.

beats: And many of them walked away.
Then he turned to his twelve
pictures: Picture 1: The Sea of Galilee at morning. Dozens of small wooden fishing boats crowded with people push toward a shore town of black basalt houses (Capernaum). On the shore, a distant tiny figure of Jesus in cream and blue-grey, back to us, walks up toward the town. Bright water, sails, energy. High wide vertical framing.

Picture 2: Inside the basalt-stone synagogue at Capernaum, packed with villagers in wool tunics and headcloths, faces turned toward the front. We see Jesus only from behind in the foreground, one hand open toward them. Dust in the shafts of light from high windows. Some faces amazed, some troubled.

Picture 3: Outside the synagogue in harsh noon light, a stream of people walking away down a dirt road, shoulders turned, some shaking their heads, a man waving a hand in dismissal. In the foreground, from behind, Jesus stands still in the doorway, not following. Long shadows.

Picture 4: Late afternoon, the twelve gathered close around Jesus (seen from behind, at the left edge). Peter, broad and bearded, steps forward with his palms open, face earnest and a little desperate. The empty road behind them. Warm low light.

Picture 5: An upper room at night, a low table with bread, a cup of wine, oil lamps. Only Jesus's hands are visible in the foreground, breaking a round flat loaf. The disciples lean in, faces lit gold by the lamps. Deep reds and browns.

Picture 6: A modern Catholic Mass in a stone church. From the back of the nave we see a priest in white vestments at the altar lifting a round white host high, candles on either side, a congregation kneeling in pews. Morning light through stained glass. Reverent, quiet, wide.

Picture 7: TODAY. A quiet empty parish church on a weekday afternoon. Lucia, 15, in her denim jacket, and Abuela in her maroon cardigan, bend a knee in the aisle facing a golden tabernacle; a small red sanctuary lamp glows beside it. Afternoon sun slants across the pews. Lucia glances at Abuela, a small warm smile.
motion: Boats bob and sails shift as the camera glides low over the water toward the shore.
Dust drifts slowly through the light beams while the camera pushes gently past Jesus's shoulder toward the crowd.
The walkers move steadily away down the road as the camera slowly pulls back from the still figure in the doorway.
Peter takes one step forward and opens his hands; slow push in on his face.
The hands slowly break the loaf in two while the lamp flames flicker; camera holds close.
The priest lifts the host slowly upward as candle flames waver; gentle push down the aisle.
The red lamp flickers softly as Lucia rises from her genuflection; slow drift toward the tabernacle.

3.story: The father who ran, the parable of the prodigal son, Luke 15:11-32; Easter night, John 20:19-23
3.point: In confession a Catholic says their sins out loud to a priest and hears out loud that God forgives them, and the priest can never tell anyone.
3.script: Jesus told a story. A young man demanded his inheritance early, left home, and blew all of it. Broke and starving, he took a job feeding pigs. So he headed home, rehearsing a speech. I've sinned. I'm not worthy to be your son. But his father saw him far off, and ran to him. Hugged him before he could finish. Threw a party. Catholics believe confession is that run. On Easter night, Jesus breathed on his friends and said: whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them. So you say it out loud, to a priest. You hear out loud: you're forgiven. And he can never tell a soul. The thing that's huge at two a.m.? Said out loud, it gets smaller.
3.drop: But his father saw him far off
beats: So you say it out loud
pictures: Picture 1: A sunlit stone farmhouse courtyard in ancient Galilee. The young son, about 19, in a rich red tunic with a gold belt, swings a heavy coin purse over his shoulder and strides out the gate without looking back. In the doorway behind, his white-bearded father in indigo watches, hand on the doorframe. Bright morning, long road ahead.

Picture 2: A muddy pig pen on a bleak hillside in a foreign land under grey skies. The son, now thin and barefoot in a torn ochre tunic, sits slumped on a fence rail holding a pail, staring at the pigs eating carob pods. Rain on the way. Lonely, wide.

Picture 3: A long dusty road at dusk. The son walks alone toward home, head down, lips moving as he rehearses, hands counting points on his fingers. His village is small and far on the horizon. Golden-pink sky.

Picture 4: The village edge at sunset. The old father, robe hitched up, runs flat out down the road, arms already open, white beard flying. Far down the road the son has stopped, startled. Villagers turn to stare. Dust kicking up in gold light. Dynamic diagonal composition.

Picture 5: A locked upper room at night, lit by one oil lamp. The disciples huddle, frightened, along the walls. In the foreground, Jesus is seen only from behind, standing among them, arms slightly raised; a soft warm light fills the room and their faces turn from fear to wonder. Peter in front.

Picture 6: Inside a modern church confessional: a wooden booth with a fine lattice screen. On one side, Grace, 16, kneels, head slightly bowed, speaking quietly; on the other side, the soft silhouette of a priest in a purple stole listens, hand at his chin. Warm low light through the lattice.

Picture 7: TODAY. Dusk on the steps of a parish church. Grace walks out, shoulders loose, breathing out, and Mateo and Lucia waiting on the steps smile and fall in beside her; Mateo holds out her coffee. The city lights coming on behind them. Easy, warm, real.
motion: The son swings the purse and strides out the gate as the camera holds on the father in the doorway.
Rain begins to fall softly and the pigs shuffle while the camera slowly pushes in on the son's tired face.
The son walks toward camera along the road as the sky slowly deepens; slight tracking back.
The father runs toward camera with arms opening and dust rising; camera tracks fast alongside him.
The lamp flame swells into a warm glow that spreads across the faces; slow push past Jesus's shoulder.
Grace speaks softly as light shifts through the lattice; very slow push toward the screen.
Grace steps down and the friends turn to join her as streetlights flicker on; gentle pull back.

4.story: Paul of Pherme and the three hundred pebbles, Palladius, Lausiac History 20; the tradition of the 'poor man's psalter'
4.point: The rosary's beads only keep count, so the hands stay busy and the mind is free to think through scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary.
4.script: In the Egyptian desert lived a monk named Paul. Every day he prayed three hundred prayers. He kept three hundred pebbles in his lap, and tossed one away with each prayer. Then he heard about a woman in a village who prayed seven hundred. He was crushed. He walked to the great old monk Macarius. Macarius said: I pray only a hundred. And my heart is at peace. The count was never the point. Later, tradition says, people who couldn't read the psalms prayed a hundred and fifty Hail Marys instead, counted on a string. That's the rosary. The beads keep the count, so your mind can walk through the lives of Jesus and Mary. The beads hanging from the mirror? Hands busy. Heart free.

open.text: three hundred *pebbles.* one for every prayer.

4.drop: Macarius said: I pray only a hundred.
beats: He walked to the great old monk
pictures: Picture 1: The Egyptian desert at dawn: pale sand dunes, a few palms, a tiny mud-brick cell. Old Paul, gaunt and bald with a long white beard and patched brown habit, sits cross-legged at the doorway, eyes closed in prayer. Vast pink-gold sky. Wide vertical framing with the monk small at the bottom.

Picture 2: Close on Paul's lap: a heap of smooth grey and white desert pebbles gathered in the fold of his brown habit. One wrinkled hand tosses a single pebble aside onto the sand, where a small scatter of others already lie. Warm side light, fine sand texture.

Picture 3: Midday outside the cell. A traveling young monk with a water skin talks and points back toward a distant village of mud houses. Paul sits frozen, the pebbles spilling from his lap, his face crushed and anxious. Hard white light.

Picture 4: The mouth of a rock cave at evening. Macarius, tiny and very old, with a wispy white beard and dark hooded robe, sits on a stone with his palm-wood staff, smiling gently and resting a hand on Paul's shoulder as Paul kneels before him. Soft amber light, calm.

Picture 5: Medieval Europe: a stone monastery on a hill where monks file into chapel with books. In the foreground field, farmers and a mother with a baby on her hip pause from work, each holding a knotted cord of beads, thumbs on the knots. Late golden light over wheat.

Picture 6: Close on young hands holding a wooden rosary, thumb on one bead. Behind and around them, softly glowing like stained glass, faint painted scenes of the lives of Jesus and Mary: a manger, a hillside, an empty tomb with light (Jesus never shown by face). Rich blues and golds.

Picture 7: TODAY. Inside a car at a red light at dusk. A wooden rosary swings from the rearview mirror. Mateo, 17, in his grey hoodie, drives; Abuela in the passenger seat rolls one bead in her fingers and looks out at the city lights, peaceful; Mateo glances at her and smiles. Warm dashboard glow, city bokeh.
motion: The sun slowly rises over the dunes as wind lifts a thin veil of sand; slow push toward the cell.
The hand tosses a pebble that lands softly in the sand; camera holds close.
Pebbles slide from Paul's lap as the traveler gestures; slow push in on Paul's face.
Macarius's hand settles on Paul's shoulder and Paul's shoulders loosen; gentle drift closer.
Wheat sways and the farmers' thumbs move along the knots; slow pan from the monastery to the field.
The thumb moves to the next bead while the glowing scenes behind brighten one by one; slight push in.
The rosary sways gently as the light turns green and the car eases forward; camera steady from the back seat.

5.story: Peter's denial by the fire, Matthew 26:58, 69-75 (the fire from Mark 14, Luke 22 and John 18)
5.point: Catholics honor the saints, imperfect people who kept getting up, and ask them to pray for us like friends, while worship belongs to God alone.
5.script: The night Jesus was arrested, his best friend Peter followed at a distance. He sat by a fire in the courtyard, warming his hands. A servant girl looked at him. You were with him. Peter said: I don't know him. Then again. Then a third time, with curses. A rooster crowed. Peter remembered, went outside, and wept bitterly. That same man is Saint Peter. The one holding the keys in church windows. Catholics count him the first pope. A saint isn't someone who never fell. It's someone who kept getting up. Catholics don't worship saints. Worship belongs to God alone. They honor them, and ask: pray for me. Like asking a friend. Living or dead, one family. That's the company you're in.

open.text: the first pope said *i don't know him.*

5.drop: That same man is Saint Peter.
pictures: Picture 1: Jerusalem at night. A line of torches moves far ahead up a stone street; among the soldiers, Jesus is only a small dark shape seen from behind. In the foreground, Peter, broad and bearded in his brown tunic, follows alone, half-hidden in the shadow of a wall, his face tense. Deep blues, orange torchlight.

Picture 2: A stone courtyard at night around a crackling fire. Servants and guards warm their hands. A young servant girl in a plain grey dress and headscarf points straight at Peter; he recoils, palms up, shaking his head. Firelight on every face, black sky above.

Picture 3: Grey-blue dawn. A rooster crows on top of a stone wall. Below it, outside the courtyard gate, Peter has fallen against the wall, face in his big hands, shoulders shaking. Soft first light, no other people.

Picture 4: Inside an old stone church, a tall stained-glass window of Saint Peter, broad and bearded, holding two great keys, gold and silver, glowing in morning sun. Below it, rows of small candles flicker on a stand. Rich reds, blues and gold.

Picture 5: A great church dome painted with a vast golden crowd of saints of every age and people: monks, mothers, fishermen, a young martyr, an old woman, Mary in blue at the center, all gathered together and looking down warmly. Seen from below, light falling from the lantern at the top.

Picture 6: TODAY. A side chapel of a parish church in the evening. Lucia, 15, in her denim jacket, lights a small candle in front of a statue of Saint Peter with keys, while Abuela beside her tucks a wooden rosary into her cardigan pocket and whispers something that makes Lucia grin. Candle glow, warm and close.
motion: Torches bob far up the street as the camera slowly follows Peter along the wall.
The fire crackles and sparks rise as the girl's arm extends and Peter pulls back; slight push in.
The rooster lifts its head to crow as the dawn light slowly grows across the wall.
Sunlight brightens through the glass and the candles flicker; slow tilt down from the keys to the candles.
Slow upward tilt and gentle rotation across the painted crowd of saints toward the light at the top.
The new candle catches and Lucia turns to Abuela, laughing softly; gentle push in.

6.story: Jesus fasting forty days and tempted in the desert, Matthew 4:1-11; Ash Wednesday words from Genesis 3:19
6.point: Lent is forty days of prayer, fasting and giving before Easter, where giving up something small makes room to notice God and other people.
6.script: Before he began his work, Jesus walked into the desert alone. Forty days. No food. At the end, he was starving. Then came the tempter. You're the Son of God? Turn these stones into bread. He didn't. He answered with the scripture: people don't live on bread alone, but on every word from the mouth of God. Hunger, it turns out, can make room. That's Lent. Forty days before Easter. It starts with a cross of ash on your forehead, and the words: remember, you are dust, and to dust you will return. Then prayer, fasting, and giving to the poor. You give up something small, and every reach for it becomes a reminder. Reach for your phone. Stop. Notice. Less, on purpose.

open.text: forty days starving. *stones* at his feet.

beats: At the end, he was starving.
pictures: Picture 1: The Judean wilderness at morning: bare tan hills, deep ravines, no plants. Jesus, seen only from behind in his cream tunic and blue-grey mantle, walks alone along a narrow ridge into the distance, very small against the huge empty land. Pale blue sky.

Picture 2: Late evening in the desert, the hills turning violet. From behind, Jesus sits on a rock, thinner now, his mantle loose on his shoulders, one hand resting on his knee, looking out over the emptiness. Cold first stars appearing.

Picture 3: Close on cracked desert ground scattered with round flat stones that look almost exactly like loaves of bread. A long, dark, cold shadow of a standing figure stretches across them from outside the frame. At the edge of the frame, Jesus's dusty sandaled feet. Harsh low light.

Picture 4: Dawn over the desert. From behind, Jesus stands tall, facing the rising sun, one open hand at his side; the bread-shaped stones lie untouched at his feet and the cold shadow is gone. The light floods gold and warm.

Picture 5: Ash Wednesday inside a modern parish church. A priest in purple vestments presses his thumb to the forehead of Grace, 16, tracing a small dark cross of ash; a line of people of all ages waits behind her, some already marked. Soft morning light, quiet.

Picture 6: TODAY. A Friday evening kitchen during Lent. Mateo, 17, sets his phone face down on the counter mid-reach, a little smile; at the table Dad Miguel, Lucia and Abuela laugh over a homemade fish dinner, a jar for coins for the poor on the windowsill. Warm lamplight, everyday and real.
motion: Wind lifts dust along the ridge as the camera slowly pulls back to reveal the empty hills.
Stars slowly appear as the light fades; the mantle shifts in a light wind; camera holds.
The dark shadow slowly lengthens across the stones; very slow push in.
The sun rises behind the figure and warm light spreads over the stones; gentle push forward.
The thumb traces the ash cross and Grace opens her eyes; camera holds close.
Mateo's hand lets go of the phone and he turns toward the table as the family laughs; slow drift in.

7.story: Juan Diego, the roses and the tilma, Our Lady of Guadalupe at Tepeyac, 1531, as told in the Nican Mopohua (traditional account)
7.point: Sacramentals are small holy things and gestures, like images, medals, holy water and palms, that are not magic but reminders pointing to God, and every family's version counts.
7.script: December, 1531. A hill outside Mexico City. Tradition says a poor Native man named Juan Diego met a lady there, who spoke to him in his own language. She asked for a church on that spot. The bishop wanted proof. So she sent Juan Diego up the bare, cold hilltop, where roses were blooming in December. He gathered them in his cloak, carried them to the bishop, and let them fall. And on the cloak was her picture. The Virgin of Guadalupe. Millions still visit that cloak. Catholics call holy things like that image sacramentals. A medal. Holy water. A palm. Your abuela's altar. Not magic. Not lucky charms. Reminders that point to God. Look around your family's house. Faith you can hold.
7.drop: And on the cloak was her picture.
pictures: Picture 1: The rocky hill of Tepeyac outside 16th-century Mexico City at dawn in winter, dry grass and cactus, a lake and the city's towers far below. Juan Diego, in white cotton and a pale agave-fiber tilma, stops on the path, looking up, as the Lady of Guadalupe appears on the slope in a turquoise star-scattered mantle and rose dress, surrounded by gold rays. Soft birdsong morning light.

Picture 2: The bishop's stone hall in early colonial Mexico City. Bishop Zumarraga, grey-bearded in a grey-brown Franciscan habit, sits at a heavy wooden table with papers, one hand raised, skeptical but not unkind. Juan Diego stands before him, hat in hand, earnest. Window light, cool tones.

Picture 3: The bare, frosty hilltop of Tepeyac at first light: grey rocks, dry thorny scrub, cold mist. In the middle of it, impossibly, a cluster of full red and pink roses in bloom, dew on the petals. Juan Diego kneels in wonder, holding open his tilma to gather them. Frost-blue and rose-red.

Picture 4: Back in the bishop's hall. Juan Diego stands and lets the corners of his tilma drop: a cascade of red and pink roses tumbles to the stone floor. The bishop and two attendants rise from their seats, startled. Warm light bursting across the room.

Picture 5: The open tilma, held up by Juan Diego's arms at the edges, reveals the traditional image of the Virgin of Guadalupe on the rough cloth: head bowed, hands joined, turquoise starred mantle, gold rays. The bishop kneels before it in the foreground, from behind. Roses at his knees. Golden glow.

Picture 6: Close, warm still-life of a family's home altarcito: a small framed Guadalupe image, a dried Palm Sunday palm tucked behind a wooden crucifix, a silver saint's medal, a wooden rosary, a plastic holy water bottle shaped like Mary, tea-light candles, marigolds and family photos. Candlelight.

Picture 7: TODAY. A cozy living room at evening. Abuela, in her maroon cardigan, lights a candle on the altarcito while Lucia sets down a new photo and Mateo, in his grey hoodie, hangs a small silver medal on his keychain, grinning at her. Grace sits on the arm of the couch, smiling. Warm lamps, phones on the coffee table, real and lived-in.
motion: Gold rays shimmer softly around the Lady as Juan Diego's tilma moves in the breeze; slow push up the path.
The bishop lowers his raised hand and leans back as dust drifts in the window light; gentle push in.
Mist drifts across the rocks and dew glistens on the roses as Juan Diego's hands reach in; slow push in.
Roses tumble from the tilma to the floor as the bishop rises; camera holds steady.
Light slowly brightens on the image as the last petals settle; very slow push toward the cloth.
Candle flames flicker and marigold petals stir; slow pan across the altarcito.
The candle catches as Mateo clips on the medal and the family laughs; gentle drift back.

sources_check: Day 1: Matthew 28:16-20 (28:17 some doubted; 28:19 the threefold name); Tertullian, De Corona 3 (tracing the sign on the forehead at every daily action); Catechism 2157

Day 2: John 6:22-69 (crowd crosses the lake, 6:24; living bread and 'my flesh', 6:51; 'this saying is hard', 6:60; many walk away, 6:66; 'Lord, to whom shall we go?', 6:68-69); Luke 22:19; Catechism 1328, 1373-1381
Day 3: Luke 15:11-32 (the prodigal son: pigs 15:15-16, rehearsed speech 15:18-19, father runs 15:20, cut off mid-speech 15:21-22); John 20:19-23 (Douay 20:23 quoted); Catechism 1422-1498, seal 1467

Day 4: Palladius, Lausiac History 20 (Paul of Pherme, 300 prayers and pebbles, the virgin with 700, Macarius with 100); 'poor man's psalter' tradition; John Paul II, Rosarium Virginis Mariae; Catechism 971, 2708

Day 5: Matthew 26:58, 69-75 (followed afar off; three denials, the third with cursing; cock crows; wept bitterly); fire from Mark 14:54, Luke 22:55, John 18:18; Apostles' Creed (communion of saints); Catechism 946-962, 971, 2132

Day 6: Matthew 4:1-11 (forty days; stones into bread; answer from Deuteronomy 8:3, paraphrased); Genesis 3:19 and the Roman Missal's Ash Wednesday formula; Code of Canon Law 1250-1253; Catechism 1434, 1438

Day 7: Nican Mopohua (traditional Nahuatl account of Guadalupe, attributed to Antonio Valeriano); Catechism 1667-1679 (sacramentals, not magic 1670, popular piety 1674-1676); Code of Canon Law 1166-1172; Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy (2001)
risks: Day 1: 'Less than two hundred years later' compresses dates: the resurrection is about AD 30 and Tertullian's De Corona about AD 211; the lesson says 'around 200'. The line 'that tiny cross grew into this one' is a simplification of a gradual history.

Day 2: The film says 'He didn't call them back' and implies Jesus meant his words literally; that is the Catholic reading the lesson itself gives, but other Christians read John 6 differently. The lines spoken by Jesus and Peter are close paraphrases of John 6:51, 6:60, 6:67-68 and Luke 22:19, not exact quotations.

Day 3: Pairing the prodigal son parable with confession ('confession is that run') is a common Catholic teaching image, not an official definition; a scholar should confirm it reads as illustration. The Easter-night quote is Douay-Rheims John 20:23 verbatim.

Day 4: Paul of Pherme's story is from the Lausiac History (early monastic literature, not scripture). 'My heart is at peace' paraphrases Macarius saying his conscience does not condemn him; in the source Macarius also gently rebukes Paul, which the film leaves out. The 'poor man's psalter' origin of the rosary is tradition, flagged as such in the script; early forms counted Our Fathers before Hail Marys.
Day 5: Matthew does not mention a fire (Mark, Luke and John do); the film blends the Gospels. Calling Peter Jesus's 'best friend' is a popular way of speaking, not a biblical phrase.

Day 6: The tempter is shown only as a shadow; check that this is acceptable. Jesus's reply is paraphrased from Matthew 4:4 (quoting Deuteronomy 8:3). The ash formula used is the Roman Missal's ('remember that you are dust'), which the lesson renders via Genesis 3:19 in Douay-Rheims.

Day 7: Guadalupe is a Church-approved apparition and Juan Diego is a canonized saint, but the Nican Mopohua's historicity is debated by historians; the script marks it as 'tradition says'. Whether the tilma image itself is properly called a 'sacramental' (it is a venerated image within popular piety) should be checked; the script says 'holy things like that image'. Depicting the Lady's apparition on screen should follow the traditional image.
